res_2b_1: Using financial and operating history alone (set A), next-year operating margin in held-out hospitals was forecast by gradient-boosted trees with an MAE of 6.65 percentage points (95% CI, 6.16-7.15) and an R² of 0.70, compared with 6.92 percentage points and 0.65 for the persistence forecast (all 3 model classes, MAE 6.65-6.92). An operating loss the next year was predicted with an AUROC of 0.93 (95% CI, 0.92-0.94) by gradient-boosted trees, similar to the persistence reference (0.93). At 2 years, the MAE was 8.14 vs 8.45 for persistence (eTable 6 in Supplement 1).
res_2b_2: Adding exposure known at forecast time did not improve any model at either horizon: 1-year MAE changed by +0.55 to +0.79 percentage points (worse) and AUROC by -0.020 to -0.003 (eTable 7 and eFigure 2 in Supplement 1), nor did realized outcome-year exposure (MAE change +0.45 to +1.15). Exposure relative to other hospitals in the same year (post hoc) changed MAE by -0.01 to +0.23 percentage points and AUROC by -0.002 to +0.001. In rolling-origin testing, 1-year MAE ranged from 6.7 to 8.1 percentage points (largest in 2020; eTable 8 in Supplement 1).
abs_2b: Next-year operating margin was forecast with a mean absolute error of 6.65 percentage points (persistence, 6.92) and operating loss with an AUROC of 0.93; adding shortage exposure did not improve either forecast.
resp_2b: With hospital-level and time-forward splits, next-year margin is forecast with an MAE of 6.65 percentage points (R² 0.70), modestly better than simply carrying forward last year's margin (6.92 percentage points; R² 0.65), and operating loss with an AUROC of 0.93.
resp_2b_short: In the revised forecasting analysis, financial history predicts next-year margin with an MAE of 6.65 percentage points, and adding shortage exposure, even perfectly foreseen exposure, does not improve it. Shortage costs appear in drug budgets (Aim 2a) but are too small relative to total expenses to move margins.
